source: 광운대 편입영어 2019~2026학년도 기출 출제 유형(문항 수·영역·문제 꼴, VocabFactory 분석)을 분석해 dailyfreetoolbox 가 새로 만든 연습 문제

passages.text: Many busy restaurants on delivery apps are, in a sense, ____. They have no dining room, no sign on the street, and often no chef of their own. These so-called ghost kitchens operate from rented industrial units, and in each one a few cooks prepare meals for several brands at once. Owners praise the model for its low rent; critics note, however, that diners rarely realize the cheerful brand on their screen shares a stove with a dozen others.

Imagine choosing tomorrow's lunch right after a large dinner. A light salad seems perfectly adequate. When we are calm and replete, we find it remarkably difficult to foresee how powerfully hunger, dread, or fatigue will sway our choices later. Psychologists call this blind spot the hot-cold empathy gap. The pragmatic lesson is to make consequential decisions in advance, while we are still ____, and to bind ourselves to them before temptation arrives.

Most people cannot tickle themselves, however hard they try. The reason lies in the brain's habit of prediction. Whenever we move, the brain forecasts the sensations that the movement will produce, and it ____ those expected sensations rather than amplifying them. A touch from someone else, by contrast, arrives unannounced and registers at full strength. Experiments with robotic arms show that even a slight delay between our own movement and the touch restores much of the tickle.

Supermarkets sometimes sell a few staple items, such as milk or eggs, for less than they paid for them. These loss leaders are hardly acts of philanthropy; the store is wagering that customers enticed by the bargain will fill their carts with other merchandise with lucrative margins. The profit on those goods more than offsets the deficit on the bargain. The strategy succeeds, however, only as long as shoppers ____. If they seize the discounted item and head straight for the checkout, the scheme simply backfires.

For decades, internet service from space had a dismal reputation. (A) Conventional communication satellites sit in geostationary orbit, about 36,000 kilometers above the equator, and circle in lockstep with the planet's rotation, appearing fixed in the sky. (B) Even at the speed of light, a signal needs about a quarter of a second to travel up and back, and this lag makes video calls awkward and online games almost unplayable. (C)
Low-Earth-orbit networks attack the problem by bringing the satellites much closer, typically a few hundred to about two thousand kilometers up; the shorter distance shrinks the delay to a level comparable with many ground-based connections. (D) Proximity, however, creates a difficulty of its own. A satellite that low races across the sky in minutes, so an operator needs thousands of them, handing each connection from one to the next, merely to keep a single subscriber online. Such constellations were long considered prohibitively expensive to build; reusable rockets and mass-produced satellites have made them ____.
The results became conspicuous after 2022, when terminals shipped to Ukraine helped sustain communications; since then the service has spread to remote farms, cargo ships, and disaster zones, reaching places that cables never served. (E) Critics observe, however, that a handful of private companies now control vital infrastructure. Governments and armed forces increasingly depend on it, raising questions that no single country can settle alone. Crowded low orbits pose another danger, threatening collisions that could scatter debris for decades; most experts therefore conclude that the skies will need rules agreed through international cooperation.

Few musical inventions have ____ as the metronome. In 1815 the inventor Johann Nepomuk Maelzel (1772–1838) patented a device that ticked out a steady beat at any speed a musician selected. A shrewd entrepreneur, he found an avid patron in Ludwig van Beethoven, who soon began adding precise metronome numbers to his scores. For the first time a composer could tell performers exactly how fast he wanted a piece to move.
Musicians have been squabbling over those figures ever since. Many of Beethoven's markings are very brisk; pianists regard some of them as nearly impossible to execute without blurring the music. Some scholars conjecture that his metronome was defective; others propose that he read the scale on the wrong side of the sliding weight. Still others point to his deafness: he may have chosen his tempos at a desk, hearing the music only in his head, where it can travel faster than fingers allow. A few performers insist that the markings mean exactly what they say, and they play accordingly with dazzling results. Most, however, conclude that the numbers should be taken with a grain of salt: they are a valuable clue to the composer's intentions, not a command to be obeyed at any cost.

Mr. Haddad and I had lived side by side for eleven years, getting along not so much like a house on fire as like ____. The trouble was a walnut tree. It stood on his side of the fence. Its branches, however, hung over my vegetable garden. They dropped leaves on my lettuces and shaded my tomatoes for most of the afternoon.
Every autumn I asked him to trim it, and every autumn he refused. His late wife had planted the tree, he said. He would not mutilate it to please a neighbor who grew vegetables anyone could buy at the market. I replied that the law allowed me to cut whatever crossed onto my property; he replied that the law did not require me to behave like a vandal. For three years we spoke only through notes taped to the fence.
Last September a storm tore off the largest branch and flung it across my garden, flattening the beans. Mr. Haddad came over at dawn with a saw. Without a word he began cutting the branch into logs. I fetched a second saw. We worked side by side until noon, sweating and saying almost nothing. When the garden was clear he looked up at the tree. It had grown too large for both our yards, he admitted.
The following week he hired a gardener to raise the crown. Now the afternoon sun could reach my tomatoes. I carried over a basket of the first ripe ones, and he invited me in for coffee. Before I left he asked a favor. Would I show him how to grow beans? His wife had always wanted a vegetable bed beneath the walnut.

For decades, many American employers have required workers to sign noncompete agreements; these contracts bar them from joining a rival or launching a competing business for a set period after they leave. The agreements were once reserved for senior executives with access to trade secrets. (A) ____, they have spread to hairstylists, warehouse staff, and fast-food employees, covering workers who know no secrets worth protecting. Critics contend that such restraints depress wages, leaving workers with little leverage to demand a raise. After all, an employee who cannot accept a better offer down the street has no bargaining chip.
In April 2024 the Federal Trade Commission voted to ban most of these agreements nationwide, estimating that roughly one in five American workers was bound by one. Business lobbies sued at once, arguing that the agency had exceeded its authority, and in August 2024 a federal judge in Texas blocked the rule before it could take effect. The struggle has since shifted to the states, producing a patchwork of rules. California has long refused to enforce most such contracts, and several other states have restricted them for lower-paid workers. (B) ____, a worker in one state may be free to change jobs; a colleague doing identical work across the border may not be. Many economists now argue that only coordinated standards across the states can end this confusion.

According to local legend, a storm in the sixteenth century uprooted a tree near Seathwaite in Borrowdale (a valley in England's Lake District). The fallen tree exposed a seam of a strange black mineral. (A) Shepherds soon discovered that it left a dark, silvery line on almost any surface and used lumps of it to mark their sheep. (B) The mineral, later named graphite, was so pure that it could be cut into sticks and used without any processing. (C) This trade made the substance very valuable. Smugglers sold stolen lumps on the ____ market, and Parliament eventually made such theft a serious crime.
England's advantage lasted until 1795. (D) That year France was at war with Britain and cut off from Borrowdale graphite. The French government asked the engineer Nicolas-Jacques Conté to find a substitute. Conté ground impure graphite into powder, mixed it with clay, and baked the paste in a kiln. (E) By changing the share of clay, he could make a lead harder or softer, and the cheap, uniform pencils soon replaced the precious English sticks across much of Europe.

When esports appeared as a medal event at the Asian Games in Hangzhou in 2023, many older spectators were baffled. Teenagers in team jerseys sat almost motionless before screens; commentators shouted, and an arena full of fans greeted each decisive maneuver like a goal. "Where exactly is the sport?" one puzzled visitor asked a reporter. For the competitors, however, the occasion was a long-awaited vindication. Competitive gaming had come a long way since 1972, the year students at Stanford University held what is often called the first video game tournament (the prize was a year's subscription to a music magazine). By the 2020s gaming had grown into an industry with professional leagues, salaried athletes, and audiences of millions. ____
Whether gaming deserves to be called a sport is a question older than it looks. Traditional sports bodies have generally defined sport by physical exertion, and skeptics point out that a player who scarcely leaves a chair can hardly be compared with a marathon runner. Defenders reply that elite players perform hundreds of precise actions per minute and train for many hours a day. Shooting and archery, they add, also demand little visible ____, yet they have long been Olympic events.
Sports federations have nonetheless been drawn in, partly for a pragmatic reason: their audiences are graying. Adolescent viewers devote far more time to gaming streams than to traditional broadcasts, and officials hope that esports will introduce them to the wider sporting world. In 2024 the International Olympic Committee announced plans for a separate Olympic Esports Games. Games that simulate real sports or involve abstract strategy have been welcomed. Titles built around realistic violence, by contrast, have been kept at arm's length.

In 2023 Detroit unveiled the first public road in the United States that can charge electric vehicles on the move. Copper coils buried beneath the pavement generate a magnetic field, which transmits energy to receivers mounted under specially equipped cars. Proponents argue that such roads could eventually let manufacturers install smaller, lighter batteries. For now, however, the technology remains ____: the pilot stretch is only about a quarter of a mile long, and few vehicles can use it.

Imagine being asked whether people in California are happier than those in the American Midwest. Most respondents in both regions say yes, citing the sunshine. Yet when researchers actually gauged life satisfaction, they found almost no difference. Psychologists call this mistake the focusing illusion: whatever we happen to be thinking about seems more ____ than it really is. Daily happiness depends far more on work, health, and relationships than on the weather.

Unlike most animals, for which freezing is lethal, the North American wood frog can ____ and emerge unscathed. As winter deepens, up to two-thirds of the water in its body crystallizes into ice. Its heartbeat ceases, and respiration halts. Glucose flooding its cells prevents them from shriveling or rupturing. In spring the frog gradually thaws and its heart resumes beating. Within hours it hops off once more in pursuit of a mate.

Buy now, pay later services let shoppers split a purchase into a few interest-free installments. Their popularity has soared among young consumers. Retailers welcome them because customers who can ____ payment tend to spend more. Critics warn that the sheer ease of such loans tempts people to juggle several plans at once and lose track of what they owe. Moreover, many of these loans have not been reported to credit bureaus, so other lenders may underestimate an applicant's existing debt.

Much of the security that shields online banking, e-mail, and software updates rests on a mathematical wager. (A) It assumes that certain problems, such as factoring an enormous number, are too laborious for any computer to solve in a useful span of time. (B) In 1994 the mathematician Peter Shor demonstrated that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could, in principle, factor such numbers with astonishing speed, threatening the codes that protect much of the internet. (C) No machine remotely capable of the feat yet exists, and estimates of when one might arrive vary widely.
Security agencies are not waiting to find out. Their worry centers on a tactic sometimes summarized as harvest now, decrypt later. An adversary could intercept and store encrypted traffic today, gambling that it can be unlocked once quantum hardware matures. Medical records, diplomatic cables, and trade secrets must remain confidential for decades; such data are therefore ____ already.
In August 2024 America's National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published its first three standards for post-quantum cryptography, ending a competition of roughly eight years. (D) The new methods rest on mathematical problems believed to withstand quantum as well as conventional attacks, and governments and technology companies have begun replacing older systems, starting with the networks that carry the most sensitive data. (E) Cryptographers caution that the new methods, too, rest on assumptions rather than proofs, and they urge organizations to design systems that can swap one algorithm for another, avoiding a costly rebuild from scratch. Data traverses borders freely, so the transition will succeed only through close international cooperation.

In 1899 the American economist Thorstein Veblen (1857–1929) published The Theory of the Leisure Class, a biting study of how the wealthy spent their money. Much of their spending, he argued, was meant not to satisfy any practical need but to display status. He coined the phrase conspicuous consumption for purchases whose chief purpose is to be seen. Examples ranged from lavish banquets to servants whose only work was to look idle on their employer's behalf.
Economists later gave his name to a curious category of products. For most goods, demand falls as prices rise. For a Veblen good, a higher price can make the item more desirable. The expense itself is part of what is being bought. Luxury watches and designer handbags are often cited as examples, and a firm that cut their prices sharply might find that buyers lost interest. The idea helps explain why some brands refuse to hold sales and why some have even destroyed unsold stock rather than let it be sold cheaply, a practice that has drawn growing criticism. For such goods, a low price would ____ the very exclusivity that customers are paying for.

For eight months the man in Apartment 4C and I had lived like ____: only a wall apart, yet we had never exchanged a word. All I knew of him was his radio, which murmured through the wall late at night. Once, unable to sleep, I had slipped a curt note under his door asking him to turn it down. The radio fell silent soon after. Then a parcel addressed simply to Apartment 4C landed on my doormat. I knocked on his door, but nobody answered, so I left a note and carried the parcel inside, intending to return it that evening.
That evening stretched into three days, and on the fourth a frail man leaning on a cane knocked on my door and apologized for the intrusion. He had discovered my note buried beneath a pile of flyers, he explained. His eyesight was failing, and he seldom ventured out after his hip operation. When I handed him the box, his face brightened. Inside were replacement parts for his only companion, which had broken a week earlier, and without it his evenings had been unbearably lonely. He added, a little sheepishly, that he would keep the volume low from now on.
I volunteered to help him install the components, and he accepted with evident relief. His apartment was a mirror image of mine, but crammed with books in four languages. While I fumbled with tiny screws, he talked about his decades as a ship's engineer. He had sailed between Gothenburg and Busan. When the radio finally crackled back to life, I told him to play it as loud as he liked. Then it dawned on me. I had lived beside this remarkable man for eight months without once learning his name.

Few trade rules show how a convenience can ____ as clearly as America's de minimis exemption. For decades, customs law let parcels worth less than a modest threshold enter the country free of duties, allowing travelers and small firms to skip most of the paperwork. In 2016 Congress raised that threshold from 200 to 800 dollars, hoping to ease trade further. (A) ____, the change produced consequences that few lawmakers had foreseen. Online platforms began shipping inexpensive clothing and gadgets directly from overseas factories to individual buyers, and the number of such parcels exploded, passing a billion a year. Customs officers could inspect only a sliver of them; domestic retailers complained bitterly, accusing foreign rivals of exploiting the rule.
In 2025 the United States ended the exemption for goods from China and then for parcels from virtually every country, forcing even cheap orders to face duties. The European Union, facing a similar flood of small packages, has moved to scrap its own duty-free threshold. (B) ____, bargain hunters on both sides of the Atlantic may soon pay more. Trade officials argue that only coordinated action among the major economies can keep the next shortcut from becoming another loophole.

The most famous hat in the tropics bears the wrong name. The so-called Panama hat has always been woven in Ecuador, mostly in the coastal town of Montecristi and the mountain city of Cuenca, from the fibers of the toquilla palm. The name stuck in the nineteenth century. At that time the hats were shipped to the Isthmus of Panama and sold to travelers and gold seekers heading for California. Demand soared anew when laborers excavating the Panama Canal adopted the light, breathable hats. A 1906 photograph of President Theodore Roosevelt wearing one at the construction site made the style fashionable in the United States.
Despite this fame, weaving remained a ____ industry, carried out by families in their own homes. A single fine hat can take a skilled weaver several months, and the tightest weaves (sometimes more than a thousand strands per square inch) are prized like jewelry. In 2012 UNESCO placed the craft on its heritage register. Weavers hope the honor will persuade a new generation to see the work as an art rather than a burden.

Few symbols on a keyboard have a stranger history than the ampersand. (A) Its shape began as a ligature, a joining of the two letters of the Latin word et, meaning and. (B) Examples of the combined form have even been found scratched on walls in Pompeii, the town buried by Vesuvius in 79 CE. (C) Over the following centuries, copyists elaborated the sign in countless ways, and so did the printers who followed Johannes Gutenberg (whose press appeared around 1450). In many typefaces the sign now scarcely resembles its two parent letters at all.
The name is younger and odder still. In nineteenth-century British and American schoolrooms, children reciting the alphabet were taught to finish not with Z but with the strange symbol, which counted as a sort of twenty-seventh letter. (D) Saying a lone and at the end of the list would have been confusing. Pupils therefore added the Latin phrase per se, meaning by itself, and chanted the words "and per se and" as one phrase. Recited rapidly by generations of children, the phrase was gradually slurred into a single word, ampersand.
Today the sign has been dropped from the alphabet. ____ Companies favor it in their names because it suggests partnership, and type designers treat it as a chance to show off, since its form is far less fixed than that of ordinary letters. (E) Some designers even judge a whole typeface by this one character. They see it as the clearest window onto the personality of the font.

Small Bluetooth trackers were designed to help owners retrieve misplaced keys and luggage, but they have also been exploited to stalk people surreptitiously. In 2024 Apple and Google introduced an industry standard to tackle the problem, so phones now warn users when an unfamiliar tracker appears to be traveling with them, whatever company made the tracker or the phone. The measure is a sobering reminder that a gadget built for convenience can readily become an instrument of ____.

Imagine facing two tasks: one is due tomorrow, while the other has no deadline but promises a far larger reward. Most people gravitate toward the first. In experiments published in 2018, participants opted for tasks described as expiring shortly. They did so despite knowing that a task with no time limit would pay more. The researchers dubbed this proclivity the mere urgency effect. Urgency, it seems, can ____ importance in our minds, which may explain why trivial e-mails so often eclipse consequential work.

Young sunflowers do not stay still. During the day their growing heads turn slowly from east to west, following the sun across the sky. At night they swing back to face east again. Once the plants mature, however, this daily dance ____: the flower heads stiffen and remain facing east. Researchers found that east-facing heads warm up faster in the morning sun and attract more visiting bees than heads turned artificially toward the west.

The first person to acquire a telephone possessed a device of negligible value because there was no one to call. Each new subscriber, however, rendered every existing phone more useful. Economists call this a network effect: the value of a product escalates with the number of people who use it. Once most of your friends have joined one messaging service, switching to a rival, however superior, means ____, so even disgruntled users tend to stay.

Most cars spend more than ninety percent of their lives parked. (A) For a gasoline car that idleness is merely wasteful; for an electric car it may be a latent asset. (B) A modern electric vehicle carries a battery large enough to power an average home for a day or more. (C) Engineers have long asked whether those batteries, sitting in driveways and parking garages, could help stabilize the electricity grid.
The concept is called vehicle-to-grid: a car tethered to a bidirectional charger would absorb electricity when it is cheap and plentiful, such as on sunny afternoons when solar panels create a glut of power. The car would then release some of it during the evening ____ hours, easing the strain when demand surges and prices soar. Spread across millions of vehicles, such a system could act like an enormous power plant, reducing the need for costly backup generators. (D)
Coordinating it, however, requires a smart grid, in which meters, chargers, and utilities exchange information continuously, allowing power flows to be adjusted minute by minute. Pilot projects in several countries have shown that the technology works. Some electric school buses already sell power back to utilities during summer vacations. Formidable obstacles remain: many drivers fear that constant charging and discharging will degrade their batteries, shortening the life of the costliest part of the car. Bidirectional chargers are also still expensive. (E) Owners must be confident that their cars will be ready when needed, and fairly paid for the service. Otherwise the idea is likely to remain hypothetical. Making it work at scale will depend on close cooperation among carmakers, utilities, and regulators.

Few art supplies have had ____ than mummy brown, a rich pigment sold to European painters for roughly three centuries. It was made, quite literally, from Egyptian mummies: ground-up human and animal remains were mixed with resin. The result was a warm, translucent color that artists prized for shadows and skin tones. The ingredient did not seem as macabre to earlier generations as it sounds, since powdered mummy had long been sold by apothecaries as a medicine, and its use in paint seemed a natural extension of that trade.
Attitudes changed in the nineteenth century, when public interest in ancient Egypt grew and more people learned what the pigment actually contained. The painter Edward Burne-Jones (1833–1898) was reportedly horrified to discover the source of his tube of mummy brown; according to his nephew, the writer Rudyard Kipling, he buried it in his garden. Buyers grew scarce; in the 1960s, by one account, a London color maker announced that it had run out of mummies to grind. Today the name survives mainly as a curiosity: a reminder that the history of art materials is sometimes stranger, and ____, than the history of art itself.

The mice of the east hedge and the mice of the west hedge had been neighbors for generations, yet they got along less like good neighbors than like ____. Late one autumn an ear of corn fell from a farmer's cart and landed in the strip of meadow between their burrows. It held enough kernels to feed both families through the winter. But it was far too heavy for one mouse, and dark clouds were gathering in the west.
Each family claimed the prize. The eldest of the east prided himself on his brawn and proclaimed that whoever moved the corn should keep it. He strained and heaved until his whiskers quivered, yet the ear did not budge. The eldest of the west scoffed at such feebleness and tried next but fared no better. One by one the others took their turns, grunting and puffing; each was convinced that the failure of the rest proved only their weakness. Each retired, exhausted and humiliated, as the clouds crept closer.
At last the smallest mouse of the west spoke up, though nobody had thought to consult her. Why, she asked, did they keep taking turns? If both families pushed at once, the ear would move. There would be more than enough for everyone. The two eldest exchanged sheepish glances. After a long pause, they agreed.
They lined up along the ear and pushed together at a signal from the smallest. The corn trundled across the meadow and into the larger burrow just as the first heavy drops began to fall. The rain drummed overhead. The two eldest mice had not spoken civilly in years, yet now they sat down side by side to work out how the kernels should be divided.

Discussing salaries has long been something of a taboo in European workplaces. Critics argue that this reticence helps camouflage persistent gaps between what men and women are paid, leaving many women underpaid for comparable work. In 2023 the campaign for equal pay won a victory when the European Union adopted a directive on pay transparency, giving member states until June 2026 to write it into national law. Under its provisions, employers will have to state a starting salary or salary range in job advertisements or before interviews. (A) ____, they may no longer ask candidates about their pay history. Employees will gain the right to request average pay levels, broken down by sex, for the same work or work of equal value. Larger companies must also report their gender pay gaps regularly, publishing figures that anyone can examine.
Supporters say the rules will strengthen the bargaining position of applicants, giving them information once held only by employers. (B) ____, some employers worry about administrative burdens, fearing friction among staff once salaries are no longer secret. Most observers expect the rules to work only if governments, employers, and unions cooperate closely.

In the early seventeenth century, Dutch ships returning home from Asia carried a cargo that dazzled Europe: blue-and-white porcelain from China. (A) Few Europeans knew how to make such hard, translucent ware, so the imported pieces fetched enormous prices at auction. (B) In 1644 China's Ming dynasty collapsed and the country was plunged into war, so exports from its great kilns slowed to a trickle. (C) Potters in the Dutch town of Delft saw their chance at once, since they already worked in tin-glazed earthenware (a softer clay covered in white glaze). (D)
They copied the Chinese patterns of dragons and flowers so well that buyers sometimes mistook their plates and bowls for the real thing. Many of the town's old breweries, left empty after local beer making declined, were turned into potteries. By the 1670s dozens of workshops were busy making such wares. (E) Delftware's ____ faded in the eighteenth century, once Chinese exports recovered and European factories learned to make true porcelain. One workshop founded in 1653 still operates today, however. Its blue-and-white tiles are still a favorite souvenir of the Netherlands.

Few travel customs are as truly Japanese as the ekiben, the boxed meal sold at railway stations. By the most common account, the first was sold in 1885 at Utsunomiya Station, north of Tokyo; it consisted of two rice balls with pickled radish, wrapped in a bamboo leaf. As the rail network spread, stations began competing to offer meals built around local specialties, which ranged from crab in the far north to beef in the central hills. A box bought on the platform became a way of tasting a region without leaving one's seat. ____
The containers themselves became part of the appeal. Vendors packed meals in clay pots, wooden boxes, and even plastic models of old trains. Collectors still prize the empty containers. Since 1966 a Tokyo department store has held an annual ekiben fair (often described as the largest of its kind), where hundreds of varieties are shipped in from across the country and crowds queue for hours. "People come to eat a journey they cannot take," one organizer told a reporter.
Speed, oddly enough, has threatened the custom it once helped to build. Bullet trains stop so briefly that vendors can no longer sell through open windows, as they did in the age of steam. In 2023 the operator of the busiest bullet-train line ended its regular trolley service. Yet the ekiben has changed rather than died out. Station shops now stock dozens of varieties. Travelers increasingly buy them before boarding, treating the meal as the first stop of the trip.

대화의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
A: I've revised this cover letter five times, and I still can't decide whether it's polished enough to submit.
B: Just bite the ____ and send it.

bite the bullet 은 '망설이던 일을 각오하고 해 버리다'라는 관용구예요. 다섯 번 고치고도 망설이는 사람에게 '눈 딱 감고 보내라'는 말이 어울려요. bite the dust 는 '실패하다·쓰러지다', bite the hand (that feeds you)는 '은혜를 원수로 갚다'라 뜻이 맞지 않고, apple·biscuit 은 bite the 와 굳은 표현을 이루지 않아요.

문장의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Travelers who book flights at the last minute during the holidays often end up paying through the ____ for cramped seats.

pay through the nose 는 '터무니없이 비싼 값을 치르다'라는 관용구예요. 연휴 직전에 표를 사면 좁은 좌석도 비싸다는 흐름에 맞아요. by the skin of one's teeth(간신히), a pain in the neck(골칫거리), keep one's chin up(기운 내다), Achilles' heel(약점)은 pay through 와 짝을 이루지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• Organizers expect the new exhibition to ____ large crowds over the holiday weekend.
• The two teams played to a ____, so neither advanced to the final round.
앞 문장은 '사람을 끌어모으다'라는 동사 draw, 뒤 문장은 '무승부'라는 명사 draw 예요. gather 는 앞 문장에만, stalemate(교착 상태)는 뒤 문장에만 맞아요. deter(단념시키다)는 사람을 끌어모은다는 뜻과 반대이고, split 은 play to a ~ 꼴로 쓰지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• The court took a ____ stance against companies that hide fees in fine print.
• After ten years at a large law ____, she opened her own practice.
앞 문장은 '단호한(firm) 태도', 뒤 문장은 '법률 회사(law firm)'예요. rigid·steady 는 앞 문장(경직된·꾸준한 태도)에는 들어가지만 law rigid, law steady 라는 말은 없어요. permissive(너그러운)는 숨은 수수료를 단속한다는 앞 문장과 반대이고, outstanding 은 뒤 문장에 맞지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.

글은 그런 일을 해낼 기계가 '아직 없다(No machine ... yet exists)'고 했어요. 이미 쓰이고 있다는 말은 글과 달라요. 쇼어의 이론적 위협, 지금 모아 나중에 푸는 수법, 2024년 표준 발표, 알고리즘을 쉽게 바꾸는 설계 권고는 모두 글에 있어요.
글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
베블런 재화는 비싸다는 것 자체가 사는 이유라서, 값을 내리면 손님이 돈을 내고 사려던 '희소함, 특별함'을 '깎아내린다(undermine)'는 말이에요. guarantee(보장하다)·multiply(늘리다)는 반대 방향이고, advertise·reward 는 글에 근거가 없어요.
Veblen thought the rich often spent money to show off status.
Veblen goods become less popular when their prices rise.
Veblen's book became a best seller among wealthy readers.
Veblen himself coined the term Veblen good.
Veblen said servants bought most luxury goods.
베블런은 부자들의 씀씀이가 필요보다 '지위를 드러내려는(to display status)' 데 있다고 봤어요. 베블런 재화는 값이 오르면 오히려 더 탐나고, 책이 부자들 사이에 잘 팔렸다는 말은 없어요. 그 이름을 붙인 것은 베블런이 아니라 '뒷날의 경제학자들'이고, 하인은 한가해 보이는 일을 하던 사람으로 나올 뿐 사치품을 사는 쪽이 아니에요.
글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
two rivals in a noisy feud
two ships moored side by side

첫 문장은 '밤에 스쳐 가는 배(ships that pass in the night)'라는 관용 비교를 비틀었어요. 콜론 뒤 '벽 하나 사이인데 말 한마디 나눈 적이 없다'가 풀이이니, 바로 옆에 '나란히 묶여 있으면서도 신호 한 번 주고받지 않는 배 두 척(two ships moored side by side)'이 맞아요. 옛 선원 친구·평생 친구는 반대 방향이고, 시끄럽게 다투는 맞수는 말 한마디 없었다는 풀이와 어긋나요.
The neighbor refused the narrator's offer of help.
The neighbor had once taught engineering at a university.
The narrator returned the parcel before leaving a note.
The neighbor's apartment was crammed with spare radio parts.
The narrator came to respect the neighbor.

소리를 줄여 달라는 쪽지까지 보냈던 글쓴이가, 이웃의 지난 삶을 듣고 라디오를 크게 틀어도 된다고 말하며 '이 대단한 사람(this remarkable man)'의 이름도 몰랐다고 깨달아요. 이런 행동으로 보아 이웃을 '존중하게 되었다'고 할 수 있어요. 이웃은 도움을 반겼고, 대학에서 가르친 것이 아니라 배의 기관사였어요. 쪽지를 먼저 남기고 사흘 뒤에 택배를 건넸으며, 집에 가득한 것은 부품이 아니라 책이에요.
글 바로 다음에 이어질 내용으로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
The narrator returns the parcel to the post office.
The neighbor moves back to Busan the following morning.
The narrator complains to the landlord about the radio.
The neighbor asks the narrator to pay for the parts.
The narrator asks the neighbor his name.
여덟 달 동안 이웃의 이름도 몰랐다는 것을 깨닫는 데서 글이 끝나요. 이어서 이름을 묻고 가까워지는 내용이 와야 해요. 택배는 이미 건넸고, 라디오를 크게 틀어도 된다고 한 뒤라 항의는 흐름과 반대이며, 이사·부품값 요구는 근거가 없어요.
글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.

첫 문장 빈칸은 글 전체를 묶는 주제문이에요. 편의를 위해 둔 소액 면세가 해외 직배송 택배 폭증으로 악용되어 결국 없어졌고, 끝 문장도 '다음 지름길이 또 다른 구멍(loophole)이 되지 않게'라고 맺으니 '구멍으로 바뀌다(turn into a loophole)'가 맞아요. 국내 소매상은 오히려 피해를 봤고, 택배는 폭증했으니 '보호'와 '온라인 쇼핑 둔화'는 반대 방향이에요. 수백 년 이어짐·모든 정부의 만족은 근거가 없어요.
글의 빈칸 (A), (B)에 들어갈 말을 가장 알맞게 짝지은 것을 고르시오.

(A) 거래를 더 쉽게 하려던 기대와 달리 '그러나(However)' 아무도 예상 못 한 결과가 나왔다는 대조예요. Moreover(게다가)·Similarly(마찬가지로)는 앞뒤가 맞서는 흐름과 어울리지 않아요. (B) 미국과 EU 가 면세를 없앤 '결과로(As a result)' 싼 물건을 찾는 소비자가 돈을 더 내게 된다는 말이에요. In contrast·Otherwise 는 앞뒤가 인과로 이어지는 흐름에 맞지 않아요.
글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.

빈칸 뒤 '가족이 자기 집에서 해 왔다(carried out by families in their own homes)'가 풀이예요. 집에서 하는 소규모 수공업인 '가내 공업(cottage industry)'이 맞아요. heavy industry(중공업)·service industry(서비스업)·defense industry(방위 산업)·fishing industry(수산업)도 industry 와 짝을 이루는 실제 용어지만 집에서 엮는 일이 아니에요.
The hats are woven quickly, usually in a single day.
Ecuador's government now exports the hats directly to Panama.
Panama hats are actually made in Ecuador, not Panama.
Roosevelt's photograph gave the hats their name.
Every Panama hat contains over a thousand strands per square inch.

이른바 파나마모자는 '늘 에콰도르에서 엮어 왔다(has always been woven in Ecuador)'고 했으니, 이름과 달리 에콰도르에서 만든다는 말이 맞아요. 좋은 모자 하나에 몇 달이 걸리고, 정부 수출 이야기는 없어요. 이름은 19세기에 이미 붙었고 루스벨트 사진(1906년)은 뒤의 일이에요. 천 가닥이 넘는 것은 가장 촘촘한 모자 '일부'예요.
글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Thus it is rarely seen in print anymore.
Because of this, companies avoid it in their names.
In fact, schools still teach it as a letter.
Yet it has hardly vanished from daily life.
Similarly, the letter Z has been dropped.

앞 문장은 알파벳에서 빠졌다는 말이고, 뒤에서는 회사 이름과 서체 디자인에 즐겨 쓰인다는 예가 이어져요. 그러니 '그래도 일상에서 사라지지는 않았다(Yet it has hardly vanished from daily life)'가 맞아요. 거의 안 보인다·회사들이 피한다는 말은 뒤의 예와 반대이고, 지금도 학교에서 글자로 가르친다거나 Z 가 빠졌다는 말은 근거가 없어요.

글의 흐름으로 보아 주어진 문장이 들어가기에 가장 알맞은 곳을 고르시오.
Such joined letters were a natural shortcut for anyone writing in haste.
주어진 문장의 Such joined letters 는 바로 앞 'e 와 t 두 글자를 이어 붙인 꼴(a joining of the two letters)'을 가리키고, 서둘러 쓰던 필경사의 지름길이었다는 설명 뒤에 '폼페이 벽에도 그 꼴이 새겨져 있다(have even been found)'가 이어져요. 그래서 (B)에 들어가요.
The sign closely resembles e and t in most typefaces.
Teachers objected when the sign was removed from the alphabet.
Children once recited the ampersand at the end of the alphabet.
Printers, not scribes, first joined e and t.
The word ampersand comes from a Greek phrase.
19세기 교실에서 아이들은 알파벳을 Z 가 아니라 이 기호로 끝맺었다고 했어요. 많은 서체에서 기호는 두 글자를 '거의 닮지 않았고(scarcely resembles)', 교사들이 반대했다는 말은 없어요. 이어 쓴 꼴은 인쇄술보다 훨씬 앞선 폼페이 벽에도 있었고, 이름은 그리스어가 아니라 라틴어 구절에서 왔어요.

대화의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
A: The printer jammed right before my presentation, and the repair will take at least an hour.
B: Relax and e-mail the slides. It's not the end of the ____.

It's not the end of the world 는 '세상이 끝나는 것도 아니다, 별일 아니다'라는 관용구예요. 발표 직전 프린터가 고장 나 당황한 사람을 달래며 슬라이드를 메일로 보내라는 말에 맞아요. the end of the line·the end of the road(막다른 끝), at the end of the day(결국), end of story(더 말할 것 없다)도 the end of 와 짝을 이루지만 '별일 아니다'라는 뜻이 아니에요.

문장의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
After a decade without a word, my old roommate phoned me out of the ____ and invited me to her wedding in Lisbon.
out of the blue 는 '느닷없이, 갑자기'라는 관용구예요. 십 년 연락이 없던 친구가 불쑥 전화했다는 흐름에 맞아요. in the red(적자인), green with envy(몹시 샘이 난), black sheep(골칫덩이), white lie(악의 없는 거짓말)는 out of the 와 짝을 이루지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• It is rarely possible to ____ a new word that an entire nation adopts.
• The referee tossed a ____ to decide which team would kick off.
앞 문장은 '(새 낱말을) 만들어 내다'라는 동사 coin, 뒤 문장은 '동전'이에요. token 은 뒤 문장에 억지로 넣을 수 있어도 '낱말을 만들다'는 뜻이 없고, fabricate(지어내다)는 앞 문장에만 들어가요. blow·copy 는 두 문장에 맞지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• We should ____ a table for six before the restaurant fills up.
• Despite her usual ____, she spoke passionately at the meeting.
앞 문장은 '예약하다', 뒤 문장은 '말을 아낌, 신중함'이라는 명사 reserve 예요. silence 는 뒤 문장에만 맞아요. deposit·portion·retain 은 '자리를 예약하다'라는 뜻이 없어요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• The climbers clung to a ____ ledge as the storm closed in.
• Without a steady income, many freelancers live in a ____ financial situation.
precarious 는 '불안정한, 위태로운'이라 폭풍 속 좁은 바위 턱과 고정 수입 없는 프리랜서의 형편 모두에 맞아요. 같은 pre-/pro- 꼴인 prosperous(번영하는)·predictable(예측 가능한)은 '고정 수입 없이'와 반대이고, preliminary(예비의)·pertinent(관련 있는)는 뜻이 맞지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• Researchers plan to ____ a survey of local farmers next spring.
• Copper is widely used in wiring because it can ____ electricity with little loss.
앞 문장은 '(조사를) 실시하다', 뒤 문장은 '(전기를) 전하다'라는 뜻의 동사 conduct 예요. administer(실시하다)는 앞 문장에만, carry(나르다)는 뒤 문장에만 어울려요. commit(저지르다)·deploy(배치하다)는 두 문장 어디에도 맞지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• Lack of sleep can be ____ to a child's ability to concentrate.
• The sudden tariff proved ____ to small exporters, many of whom went bankrupt.
detrimental to 는 '~에 해로운'이라 수면 부족과 파산을 부른 관세 두 곳에 다 맞아요. beneficial(이로운)·conducive(도움이 되는)는 반대이고, insensitive·respectful 은 사람의 태도를 나타내는 말이라 맞지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• Astronomers gathered on the hilltop to ____ the rare eclipse.
• All drivers must ____ the speed limit in school zones.
앞 문장은 '관찰하다', 뒤 문장은 '(규칙을) 지키다'라는 뜻의 observe 예요. perceive 는 앞 문장에 맞을 뿐 '규칙을 지키다' 뜻이 없고, heed(주의를 기울이다)는 뒤 문장에만 맞아요. reflect·deserve 는 두 문장 모두에 맞지 않아요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• With prices climbing so quickly, an interest rate hike seemed ____.
• Some friction is ____ when five people share a cramped office.

inevitable 은 '피할 수 없는'이라 물가가 뛰니 금리 인상은 '피할 수 없어 보였다', 좁은 사무실에서 마찰은 '피할 수 없다' 두 곳에 다 맞아요. 생김새가 비슷한 invincible(무적의)은 뜻이 다르고, improbable(있을 것 같지 않은)은 반대예요. imminent(임박한)는 앞 문장에, routine(흔한)은 뒤 문장에만 어울려요.

두 문장의 빈칸에 공통으로 들어갈 말로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
• The old market street is ____ for pickpockets, so keep your wallet in a front pocket.
• The senator is ____ for arriving late to every committee meeting.
notorious for 는 '(나쁜 일로) 악명 높은'이라 소매치기가 많은 거리와 늘 늦는 의원 모두에 맞아요. renowned(이름난)·exemplary(모범적인)는 좋은 뜻이라 반대이고, accountable for 는 '~에 책임이 있는', susceptible 은 to 와 쓰여 뜻이 맞지 않아요.
I want that you finish it by Friday.
My parents wouldn't allow me going abroad.
He persuaded me buying a refurbished laptop.
The guards prevented him to enter the embassy.
The cardiologist advised him to cut down on salt.
advise 는 목적어+to부정사를 받아 맞아요. allow·persuade 도 목적어 뒤에 to부정사(to go, to buy)가 와야 하고, want 는 that 절이 아니라 want you to finish, prevent 는 prevent him from entering 꼴이에요.
There were much luggages at the airport.
I wish I can visit Paris again next year.
If he would have asked, I would have helped him.
She gave me some invaluable advice about the interview.
He bought two new furnitures for his spacious apartment downtown.
advice 는 셀 수 없는 명사라 some invaluable advice 가 맞아요. furniture·luggage 도 셀 수 없어 two pieces of furniture, a lot of luggage 처럼 써요. wish 뒤에는 can 대신 could, 과거 일을 가정하는 if 절은 had asked 여야 해요.
He insisted to pay for the banquet.
The news were astounding to everyone.
I'm looking forward to meet your family.
Not knowing what to say, she remained silent.
Walking down the street, the rain started to fall.
분사구문의 부정은 Not 을 앞에 두고, 말을 몰랐던 주체도 she 라 맞아요. 길을 걸은 것은 비가 아니라 사람이라 주어가 어긋나고, insist 는 insisted on paying, look forward to 뒤는 meeting, news 는 단수라 was 여야 해요.
I wish I am as tall as my older brother.
The documentary was so bored that I left early.
The broth was too salty for the toddlers to eat.
He didn't run enough fast to catch the last bus.
It was a such beautiful day that we went to the beach.
too ~ for+의미상 주어+to부정사 꼴이 맞게 쓰였어요. such 는 a 앞에 와서 such a beautiful day, enough 는 부사 뒤에서 fast enough, 다큐멘터리는 지루함을 '주는' 쪽이라 boring, 이루기 어려운 바람을 나타내는 wish 뒤에는 am 대신 were 가 와야 해요.
He will call you as soon as he gets home.
I have known her since we were adolescents.
When I arrived, the meeting already finished.
She was simmering the stew when the phone rang.
By next June, I will have worked here for ten years.
내가 도착한 때보다 회의가 먼저 끝났으므로 과거완료 had already finished 가 되어야 해요. since 와 현재완료, 시간 부사절의 현재 시제 gets, 미래완료, 과거진행은 모두 맞아요.
I'll give you whatever you need.
What matters most is your health.
This is the reason why I left early.
She is the mentor which I trust most.
The house whose roof leaked was sold.
선행사가 사람(the mentor)이라 which 가 아니라 who(m)나 that 을 써야 해요. 주어 자리 What 절, 소유격 whose, the reason why, whatever 는 맞아요.
The letter was written in French.
The children were told to wait in the hall.
This lullaby is cherished by people of all ages.
The museum is consisted of three spacious galleries.
A suspension bridge is being built across the estuary.
consist of 는 자동사라 수동태로 쓰지 않아요(The museum consists of three galleries). 진행 수동 is being built, 수동 were told to wait 와 is cherished by 는 맞아요.
He vowed to call me back.
It is worth visiting the old palace.
We are considering to move to the countryside.
consider 는 동명사를 목적어로 받아 considering moving 이 되어야 해요. relish+동명사, remember -ing(한 일을 기억하다), vow+to부정사, be worth -ing 는 맞아요.
I'll wait here until you come back.
She has worked here for five years.
During the flight, I watched two movies.
While the flight, I slept most of the time.
We stayed indoors all weekend because of the heavy blizzard.
while 은 접속사라 뒤에 절이 와야 해요. 명사 the flight 앞에는 전치사 During 을 써야 해요. During+명사, until+절, for+기간, because of+명사는 맞아요.
Had I known, I'd have called.
This is the hotel we stayed at.
Everyone in the firm was invited.
